title: Event-Driven Systems and Stream Processing

sections.title: Following an Order Through the Notification Pipeline
Choosing a Queue or a Retained Log
Submitting Email to an External Provider
When Skipping a Record Breaks Ordering

html:
A customer can finish placing an order at Baodium and receive a confirmation on the page before the email arrives. That is usually what we want. The customer should not have to wait for an email provider to accept a message before learning whether the purchase succeeded. But what happens when the email still has not arrived half an hour later?

During a promotion, support began receiving those complaints. Checkout was healthy, orders were committing, and Kafka showed almost no consumer lag. The notification dashboard even reported that nearly every order event had been processed. An engineer proposed adding more consumers, expecting the email service to be falling behind. Another engineer opened the notification database and found several hundred thousand unfinished email tasks.

The two dashboards were describing different parts of the same workflow. Notification Service had read the events and recorded the tasks. Its sender workers were submitting those tasks to the email provider at about 10,000 per minute, while new tasks were arriving at 12,000 per minute. Kafka could be completely caught up while customers continued waiting for confirmation emails.

That incident brings together the decisions we made in earlier chapters. Chapter 3 introduced durable operations and the transactional outbox. Chapter 4 removed email delivery from the synchronous checkout path. Chapter 11 gave Catalog its own data authority and allowed search to maintain a projection from published changes. All three decisions left some processing to happen after the original request, sometimes on another machine and sometimes more than once.

We need to know when that processing has finished, how it recovers after an interruption, and whether the next attempt could repeat a business effect. Baodium’s notification pipeline gives us a useful example because each stage has its own durable state, capacity limit, and failure behavior.

Following an Order Through the Notification Pipeline

The original checkout handler called the email provider before returning to the customer. When the provider was slow, checkout was slow. A provider error could even produce a failed HTTP response after the order had already committed, leaving the customer uncertain about whether to submit again.

The revised path has four stages.

  1. Order Service commits the confirmed order and a notification outbox record in one PostgreSQL transaction.

  2. An outbox relay publishes the committed event to Kafka.

  3. Notification Service consumes the event and creates a durable email task in its own database.

  4. Sender workers submit due tasks to the email provider and record what the provider reports.

Order Service can now confirm the purchase without waiting for the last three stages. If Kafka is unavailable, the outbox record is still present. If Notification Service crashes after reading an event, Kafka can deliver that event again. If the email provider is unavailable, the task waits in Notification Service’s database for another permitted attempt.

That arrangement gives each stage a recovery path. It also means a successful result from one stage cannot establish that all later stages have finished.

What Does Processed Mean?

During the promotion, the metric called events_processed_total was rising normally. It measured the transaction that created an email task, because that was the consumer’s responsibility. The counter was accurate, but its name invited the reader to assume the email had been sent.

For this workflow, submitted means that Notification Service has recorded the provider’s acceptance against the task. A later delivery report may establish that the message reached the recipient’s mail server, and a bounce may establish that delivery failed. Neither provider acceptance nor a delivery report proves the recipient read the email.

The sender dashboard therefore reported accepted submissions, definitive failures, uncertain outcomes, and overdue unfinished tasks. A latency chart built only from successful submissions would exclude customers whose tasks were still waiting. The age of the oldest unfinished task was just as important as the time taken by tasks that had already completed.

Backlog Growth During the Promotion

The sender’s capacity problem becomes clearer when we calculate the rate at which unfinished work accumulated. New notification tasks arrived at 12,000 per minute. The provider accepted 10,000 per minute, giving a net increase of 2,000 unfinished tasks each minute.

After three hours at those sustained rates, the backlog would contain approximately

180×2,000=360,000180 \times 2{,}000 = 360{,}000180×2,000=360,000

unfinished tasks. If no new tasks arrived, senders processing 10,000 per minute could clear that backlog in 36 minutes. During a promotion, new orders would continue arriving.

Suppose the provider increased Baodium’s allowance and sender throughput rose to 14,000 per minute while arrivals continued at 12,000. Only 2,000 completions per minute would reduce the existing backlog. Clearing 360,000 tasks would then take three hours. We can express that estimate for a backlog BBB, new-task rate λ\lambdaλ, and completion rate μ\muμ:

Tdrain=Bμ−λ,μ>λ.T_{\mathrm{drain}} = \frac{B}{\mu-\lambda}, \qquad \mu>\lambda.Tdrain​=μ−λB​,μ>λ.

The estimate assumes reasonably stable arrival and completion rates. A provider outage during recovery or a wave of retries would change them. The completion rate also needs to count distinct tasks reaching their required outcome. Counting every HTTP attempt as a completion could make a repeatedly failing sender appear productive.

Why Age Matters Alongside Depth

Figure Figure compares backlog conditions that can have similar counts but different trends.

If tasks were served strictly in arrival order, the oldest unfinished task after those three hours would be roughly thirty minutes old. Senders working at 10,000 per minute would have completed tasks from the first 150 minutes, leaving the most recent thirty minutes of arrivals.

Actual senders run concurrently. Some tasks fail and wait for retries, while others are submitted immediately. An old task can remain unfinished long after the general queue has moved on. Baodium therefore measured age directly from durable task records instead of deriving it from the backlog count.

The dashboard also separated first submissions from retries. If most new tasks finished promptly but a few hundred repeatedly failed with the same provider error, additional sender processes would not fix those tasks. If every task was late and the provider was already at its agreed rate, the team had to reduce eligible arrivals or obtain more provider capacity. More Kafka consumers would not change either limit.

Decision review

Which stage should Baodium scale?

Kafka consumer lag is close to zero. Notification Service creates 12,000 tasks per minute, while the provider accepts 10,000 per minute. After three hours, approximately 360,000 tasks are unfinished. The provider’s current rate allowance may be the limiting factor.

Double the Kafka task-creator consumers.

Double sender workers without changing the provider allowance.

Verify the provider limit, protect confirmation capacity, and reduce optional email traffic or obtain a higher accepted rate.

The first choice adds capacity to a stage that is already caught up. The second helps only if sender execution is the bottleneck and the provider can accept more requests. If the provider’s allowance is already fully used, more senders may generate rate-limit rejections and retries.

The third choice addresses the binding constraint. Optional marketing messages can be deferred under their separate contract, while accepted order confirmations remain durable. If all 12,000 new tasks are required confirmations, arrivals cannot simply be discarded. The team needs more provider capacity, a longer declared completion interval, or bounded refusal of new work under the product’s admission policy.

Choosing a Queue or a Retained Log

The notification pipeline used Kafka between Order Service and Notification Service. That choice is easier to evaluate when we compare it with a durable work queue.

In a traditional work-queue design, a group of workers competes to receive tasks. After the successful acknowledgment, a task no longer needs to be available for the normal delivery path. RabbitMQ and Amazon SQS can support this kind of worker coordination, with their own delivery, visibility, and retention rules.

A retained log has a different access model. Kafka appends records to partitions and keeps them according to topic retention. Each consumer group tracks its own position. Notification Service and Analytics can read the same order event independently, and Analytics can start later and process older events while those events are still retained.

This does not make Kafka a required component of every asynchronous system. If the only downstream action is sending one email, a durable notification table and a managed queue may be enough. Baodium used a retained event log because independent consumers also needed order facts for analytics, auditing, and other projections. The decision depended on those requirements, along with the operational cost of running the broker.

Retention and Compaction

Kafka does not wait for every consumer to finish before deleting old events. A topic configured for fourteen days of time-based retention can remove records even if one consumer group has been unavailable throughout that period. After deletion, resetting the group’s offset cannot retrieve those records. Recovery needs another source, such as an archive or a rebuild from the owning service’s authoritative state.

Kafka also supports log compaction. On a compacted topic, later records for a key can replace earlier ones during background cleanup. A product-state topic keyed by product ID can therefore help rebuild a projection from the latest retained state for each product. Compaction is asynchronous, so older versions may still be present until cleanup runs. It does not provide a complete historical record of price changes.

Deletes need special handling. A compacted topic usually represents a deletion with a null-valued record called a tombstone. Tombstones are retained for a configured interval and can later be removed. A slow rebuild that misses them could incorrectly restore a product that was deleted. Baodium sized tombstone retention and rebuild time together and verified the resulting projection against Catalog.1

# Events retained for 14 days
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create \
  --topic order-events --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config retention.ms=1209600000 \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2

# Latest product state, with tombstone retention configured
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --create \
  --topic product-state --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config cleanup.policy=compact \
  --config delete.retention.ms=604800000 \
  --config min.insync.replicas=2

The commands assume a Kafka cluster with enough brokers for a replication factor of three. The product-state topic uses seven days of delete-marker retention as an example. That period needs to exceed the tested time for an approved consumer to rebuild and catch up, with appropriate margin.

Retention for ordinary event topics must cover detection, diagnosis, repair, and catch-up. A consumer may fail on Monday, need two days for repair, and require another day to replay its backlog. A two-day topic retention would be insufficient. Baodium’s fourteen-day policy provided more time for recovery, but it was still a bound that the team monitored.

Partitions, Offsets, and Consumer Groups

Kafka splits a topic into partitions, which can be processed independently. Each record has an offset identifying its position within one partition. Consumers belonging to the same group divide the partitions among themselves and commit offsets so processing can resume after a restart.

With twelve partitions and four active consumers, the group can assign three partitions to each consumer. With twelve consumers, each can receive one. A thirteenth consumer has no partition to process in that topic. Adding more consumers beyond the partition count therefore does not increase ordinary group parallelism for that topic.

The committed offset is usually the next record the group should resume from. After durably processing offset 42, the consumer commits 43. The records it fetched and its committed position are separate. That distinction matters during failure, as we will see shortly.

Keys and Per-Order Ordering

Kafka preserves the order of records within a partition. It does not establish an order across all partitions in a topic. Baodium used order_id as the Kafka record key so that events for one order were routed to the same partition under a stable partitioning rule.

That supports per-order ordering when the publisher also sends those events in the intended order. The broker cannot repair a producer that publishes OrderShipped before OrderConfirmed. It stores the records in the order it receives them. Nor does keying alone stop consumer code from completing two records concurrently in the opposite order.

The key also determines where throughput concentrates. If all events for a very busy tenant use one tenant ID as the key, they reach one partition. Adding consumers cannot divide that tenant’s stream further. The appropriate key depends on the required ordering boundary, just as the shard key in Chapter 7 depended on which records needed to change together.

Increasing a topic’s partition count introduces a less obvious risk. Under common keyed partitioning algorithms, a record’s assigned partition can change when the partition count changes. An order’s older events may still be waiting in the original partition while newer events are written to another. Systems requiring strict per-order processing need a controlled topic migration, stable mapping, or another ordering protocol rather than assuming a partition increase is transparent.

Whole State and Incremental Changes

Consumers also need to know what an out-of-order event contains. Suppose a search projection receives a complete product snapshot at version 12 before receiving version 11. If version 12 contains the full state needed by the projection, it can apply 12 and later ignore 11.

A different event might say PriceReducedByFiveDollars. Applying version 12 while version 11 is missing could produce the wrong price. A consumer of incremental changes must detect the gap, retrieve or wait for missing changes, or reconcile from the authoritative source. The event contract should say whether an event is a full replacement or an incremental operation.

Publishing Events Without Losing Them

We can now return to the outbox relay. Order Service writes an event into its local database transaction, but the event still needs to reach Kafka. The relay cannot atomically commit a PostgreSQL transaction and a Kafka append as one ordinary local transaction.

Each outbox event has a stable message identity and enough information for consumers to interpret it. The relay does not generate a new identity when it retries a publication.

{
  "message_id": "3f0c9a6e-2c41-4f7b-9d8e-5b1a7c2e4f10",
  "event_type": "OrderConfirmed",
  "schema_version": 2,
  "occurred_at": "2026-03-14T10:00:03.214Z",
  "order_id": "ord_4471",
  "order_version": 3,
  "payload": {
    "customer_ref": "cus_88213",
    "total_minor_units": 12950,
    "currency": "USD"
  }
}

The message_id recognizes duplicate delivery. The event type and schema version describe the payload, while the order version helps a consumer detect missing or out-of-order transitions. The order ID becomes the Kafka key. The occurred_at timestamp describes the business action, which may be earlier than broker publication.

CloudEvents provides a standardized envelope with corresponding fields such as id, source, type, and time. Baodium could use that convention without changing its underlying outbox or consumer guarantees.

The Relay’s Uncertain Acknowledgment

The relay reads unpublished outbox rows, publishes them, waits for Kafka’s acknowledgment, and records publication success. Now consider a crash after Kafka accepted the event but before PostgreSQL recorded the acknowledgment. The row remains unpublished locally. The restarted relay sends the same event again, and Kafka can contain two copies of the business message.

Recording publication in PostgreSQL before Kafka acknowledges it would be worse: the relay might lose an event without leaving an unpublished row to recover. Baodium chose possible duplicate publication and required consumers to deduplicate by stable message identity.

This is the persistent record and the starting query for a relay. The complete worker also needs bounded ownership of rows it is publishing. It must not hold a PostgreSQL transaction and its row locks open across a slow Kafka network call. Baodium used short database claims, an expiring relay lease, and guarded publication updates. A claim that expires must not allow an older worker to overwrite the newer owner’s state. These are the leasing and fencing rules from Chapters 3 and 7.

The oldest unpublished row and its age were important health signals. An outbox backlog can increase while Kafka consumer lag remains low, because the events have not reached Kafka at all.

Preserving Order With Several Relays

Adding relay processes can increase publication throughput, but a naïve use of FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED can reorder events for one order. One relay may claim OrderConfirmed, pause, and let a second relay claim and publish OrderShipped. The Kafka key sends both to the same partition but cannot change the order in which they arrived.

Baodium assigned each order to a stable relay shard. Only one relay had publication authority for a shard at a time, and replacement required fencing the previous owner. The relay published an order’s events in version order, completing or resolving an uncertain publication before moving to the next version for that order. Where Kafka transactions were used for the relay, a stable transactional.id for each shard allowed the new producer to fence an earlier producer instance. The application still checked its database ownership epoch.

Order Service serialized changes to each order and wrote the business transition and its outbox event in the same transaction. Its sequence of committed order versions therefore defined the intended event order. A PostgreSQL BIGSERIAL value by itself does not prove commit order across unrelated transactions, so the relay did not rely on a sequence number alone to establish per-order correctness.

An alternative is change-data capture through a system such as Debezium, which reads committed database changes and can publish outbox records without the polling relay. It requires its own replication-slot, connector, routing, and failure policies. Chapter 11 examined the retained-WAL risk when a logical replication consumer stops progressing.

Kafka Producer Durability

Baodium configured the outbox producer to request acknowledgments from all in-sync replicas and enabled producer idempotence.

acks=all
enable.idempotence=true
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5
delivery.timeout.ms=120000

The topics used three replicas and min.insync.replicas=2. Together with acks=all, these settings require the configured minimum number of in-sync copies before Kafka acknowledges a new record. They improve durability, although the recovery behavior also depends on leader election, replica health, and the cluster’s settings. The broker cannot acknowledge new writes at the required level if too few in-sync replicas are available.

Producer idempotence protects against duplicates generated by retries of the same producer’s sends under its producer identity and sequence numbers. It does not recognize a business event that a restarted relay sends again as a new publication. Its message_id and the consumer’s local transaction are what protect the downstream effect across those restarts.2

Committing Consumer Progress

Notification Service uses a Kafka consumer group to turn each OrderConfirmed event into a durable email task. Its processing position in Kafka is independent of the transaction that writes the task to PostgreSQL.

Imagine the consumer receives offset 42. It creates the task and commits its database transaction, then crashes before committing Kafka offset 43. After restart, Kafka delivers offset 42 again. That is acceptable if the consumer recognizes the event and does not create another task.

Now reverse the order. If the consumer commits offset 43 first and crashes before creating the task, the group can resume at 43 and omit the task. Baodium committed the database effect before advancing the Kafka offset. That gives at-least-once processing under the retention and recovery contract, including the possibility of redelivery.

Consumer Configuration

The consumer disabled automatic offset commits because those could advance independently of its database transaction. The following settings illustrate the notification task creator’s policy.

group.id=notification-task-creator
enable.auto.commit=false
auto.offset.reset=earliest
isolation.level=read_committed
max.poll.records=200
max.poll.interval.ms=300000
partition.assignment.strategy=\
  org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor

auto.offset.reset=earliest applies when the group has no valid committed offset. It does not rewind an existing consumer group every time that consumer starts. read_committed omits aborted transactional records when the producer uses Kafka transactions. It does not make Notification Service’s PostgreSQL transaction part of Kafka’s transaction.

The cooperative assignment strategy can reduce the number of partitions revoked during a rebalance. Static membership through a unique, stable group.instance.id can also reduce reassignment during short restarts when supported by the deployed client and group protocol. Different instances must never share the same instance ID. Neither setting removes the need to tolerate redelivery.

Creating Each Notification Task Once

The task creator needs two kinds of duplicate protection. A message ID identifies one published event, so it can be recorded in a processed-event table. A business constraint also prevents two independent events from creating two initial confirmation tasks for one order.

Both the deduplication marker and task creation belong in one PostgreSQL transaction. If the transaction fails, both changes roll back and the redelivered event may try again.

This example processes records sequentially within a partition. A worker that processes records concurrently must commit only through the first contiguous sequence of completed records. If offset 42 finishes while 41 is still running, committing 43 would allow a restart to skip 41.

The database claim uses one atomic insert rather than a read followed by an insert, which would race under concurrent redelivery.

The insert returns a row only for a newly claimed event. The transaction inserts the task when that happens. If a different message ID already created the order-confirmation task, create_confirmation_once must handle the business uniqueness conflict safely in that same transaction. A uniqueness error that aborts the transaction without being handled would also roll back the event claim. Both behaviors can be made correct, but the repository must implement one deliberately.

The producer assigns message_id once in the outbox. Retrying publication preserves it. Deduplication records must survive for as long as the system permits redelivery or replay. Removing old markers while retaining replayable business events can make an old event look new again.

Submitting Email to an External Provider

The database constraint can guarantee that Baodium records one initial confirmation task per order. It cannot guarantee that the email provider accepts only one submission. A sender may submit the email, lose the response, and have no local evidence of acceptance.

Some providers support submission idempotency and status lookup by a stable client key. Where that contract exists, Notification Service uses the task’s durable identity for every submission and checks the provider before repeating an uncertain attempt. The key’s scope and retention must be documented. If the provider offers neither guarantee, Baodium must explicitly choose between the risk of a duplicate email and the risk of an omitted one.

That is a different business decision from charging a card twice, but it is still a decision the engineering team should not delegate to the default retry behavior of an HTTP library.

Sender State and Recovery Leases

The sender database records whether a task is waiting, being sent, accepted, scheduled for retry, uncertain, or permanently failed. The states are PENDING, SENDING, ACCEPTED, RETRY_SCHEDULED, UNCERTAIN, and FAILED. Recipient delivery reports are recorded separately from provider acceptance.

Several workers may claim tasks concurrently. A short database transaction selects due tasks with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, records a lease owner, expiry, and incremented claim version, then commits before contacting the provider.

The task schema includes the lease owner, lease expiry, claim version, next-attempt time, and attempt count, with appropriate defaults. A result update checks the current lease owner, version, and allowed state before applying the provider’s outcome. That prevents an old worker whose lease has expired from overwriting a newer worker’s local decision.

Lease expiry does not cancel a provider request already in progress. When recovery finds an expired SENDING task, it marks the outcome UNCERTAIN rather than assuming the email was never accepted. It then follows the provider’s status or idempotent-retry contract. If no safe recovery operation exists, the task may require an explicit manual decision under the notification policy.

Retrying a Known Temporary Failure

A definitive temporary rejection can be scheduled for another attempt. The sender uses exponential backoff with full jitter: after each failed attempt, it chooses a random delay between zero and a maximum that grows exponentially, up to a configured cap.

delay∼Uniform⁡(0,min⁡(cap,base×2n)).\text{delay} \sim \operatorname{Uniform} \left(0,\min(\text{cap},\text{base}\times 2^{n})\right).delay∼Uniform(0,min(cap,base×2n)).

Here nnn is the retry number starting at zero. With a ten-second base and fifteen-minute cap, the sixth retry (n=5n=5n=5) can wait up to 320 seconds. The task’s maximum age and attempt count still determine when it is marked FAILED.

A fixed five-minute delay would be risky if ten thousand tasks failed during the same minute of a provider outage. They could all return at the same time just as the provider recovered. Jitter spreads those attempts, while the rate limiter and retry budget from Chapter 9 keep their combined demand within the provider allowance. Waiting tasks do not occupy sender threads or provider-call permits between attempts.

Locating the Actual Backlog

The notification incident becomes easier to investigate once each stage reports the work it has accepted and the work it has completed.

Kafka consumer lag is the difference between a partition’s log-end offset and the group’s committed offset. It describes progress through the retained log, ending at whatever durable point the consumer uses before committing. It says nothing about a notification task waiting in a separate sender database.

The on-call engineer compared Kafka offsets with unfinished tasks.

$ kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
    --describe --group notification-task-creator
TOPIC         PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG
order-events  0          8812410         8812416         6
order-events  1          8790233         8790233         0

-- Run separately in the notification database
SELECT state, count(*) AS tasks,
       now() - min(created_at) AS oldest
FROM notification_tasks
WHERE state NOT IN ('ACCEPTED', 'FAILED')
GROUP BY state;

A few offsets of lag in Kafka alongside hundreds of thousands of unfinished database tasks identified the sender stage as the bottleneck. The team checked the provider’s rate allowance before adding workers. More senders would help only if the application itself was the limiting stage. If the provider was already accepting the maximum permitted rate, more workers would produce more refusals and retries.

Lag also needs to be examined per partition. A small average can conceal one partition that has stopped progressing. Offset count alone is not a time measurement: a thousand records can represent seconds on a busy partition or hours on a quiet one. When the completion objective is expressed in minutes, the age of unfinished work and observed processing progress are more useful alert signals.

Rebalancing and In-Flight Work

Consumer-group membership changes during deployments and failures. Kafka may reassign a partition from one consumer to another in a rebalance. Suppose consumer A creates the task for offset 500 but loses partition ownership before committing its progress. Consumer B may begin from the previous committed offset and read 500 again. The database’s event claim and business constraint prevent another task.

The complication grows when the consumer hands records to background workers. Calling poll() regularly can prevent a long operation from exceeding max.poll.interval.ms, but continued polling does not make a background result safe to commit after the partition has been revoked. The consumer tracks completed offsets per partition and stops admitting new work for partitions it no longer owns. Rebalance callbacks coordinate shutdown or handoff of remaining records.

Cooperative reassignment and static membership can reduce disruption. They cannot eliminate redelivery when a process crashes between the business transaction and the offset commit. The core recovery contract therefore remains the same regardless of the assignment strategy.

Permanent Failures and Dead-Letter Records

Some failures clear after another attempt. A temporary database outage or a rate-limited provider may justify bounded retries. Other failures, such as a malformed event or an unsupported schema version, are unlikely to improve by repeating the same input.

A consumer cannot simply acknowledge a permanently failing record and forget it. Baodium preserved the original bytes, topic, partition, offset, schema metadata, and failure reason in a controlled dead-letter path. It confirmed durable storage of the failed record before advancing the source offset. If that confirmation was uncertain, the record could be stored again after restart, so the dead-letter consumer also used a stable failure identity for deduplication.

A dead-letter topic makes failed records available for inspection and repair. It does not mean their business effects have completed. The notification team assigned an owner and alert to the oldest unresolved dead-letter record, with access restrictions for potentially sensitive payloads.

When Skipping a Record Breaks Ordering

Suppose OrderConfirmed cannot be decoded and is sent to a dead-letter topic. The next record for the same order is OrderShipped. If the consumer processes that second event without checking state, its projection may describe a shipped order it never recorded as confirmed.

The team had three reasonable approaches. It could pause the whole partition, accepting that unrelated orders would also wait. It could persist a block for that order while continuing other keys, provided its scheduling and offset-commit design preserved the block across restarts. Or it could reconcile with Order Service’s authoritative state and rebuild the order projection before proceeding.

The right response depends on what the consumer promises. A confirmation email task may be created directly from OrderConfirmed, while an order-state projection must preserve a valid transition history. A generic “send to dead letter and continue” rule is insufficient for both.

Replay and Schema Evolution

Kafka retention permits consumers to read older records again. That is useful for rebuilding a search projection after a bug. It is dangerous when replay causes external effects, such as sending emails or charging payments.

For a projection rebuild, Baodium created a new destination and a new consumer group configured to begin at the earliest retained offsets. The worker processed the snapshot or compacted state and subsequent events, compared the result with the authoritative source, then changed read routing after validation. The original consumer remained available until the replacement met its freshness requirement.

The kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets command is for changing offsets of a selected consumer group when its members are inactive. A brand-new group usually does not need that command. It can start at the earliest retained offset through its consumer configuration. For an existing inactive rebuild group, the reset can be previewed before execution.3

kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 \
  --group catalog-projection-rebuild-2 \
  --topic product-state --reset-offsets --to-earliest

# After verifying the preview, execute the same command with:
# --execute

Replaying the notification consumer with expired deduplication markers could create new tasks for old orders. Baodium did not use ordinary replay to resend a customer’s confirmation. A corrected email required a new, authorized repair operation with its own identity and audit trail.

Old Events and Changed Meaning

A new consumer may encounter event versions written months earlier. A schema registry can validate selected compatibility rules, but the application still has to interpret older values correctly.

Consider a field named discount_applied. If an old event lacks that field, it may mean the order had no discount, or it may mean the producer did not record discounts at that time. Those interpretations produce different financial totals.

A subtler change keeps the same field name and type but changes its meaning from gross amount to net amount. Structural schema validation can pass while reporting becomes wrong. The event contract therefore records semantic versions or distinct field names for changes in meaning, and consumer tests include examples from every retained schema version.

The same rule applies to event time and correction records. A projection rebuild must know whether a later message replaces earlier state or adds another amount, and it must account for events missing from Kafka because retention or compaction has already removed them.

Stateful Stream Processing

Notification Service creates one task from one order event. Some consumers need to combine many events. Baodium’s merchant analytics service calculated five-minute order totals by merchant, while fraud monitoring examined activity over longer windows.

A running total is application state. Suppose the processor adds a $120 order to a merchant’s total and crashes before recording its input position. After restart, reading the event again would add another $120 unless the processor restores the state and source position consistently.

Kafka Streams and Apache Flink provide mechanisms for stateful processing and recovery. Depending on their configuration, they can checkpoint state and input progress together and restore that consistent position after a failure. An end-to-end exactly-once claim also depends on the sink. A framework cannot atomically include an unrelated email or payment provider in its checkpoint without a corresponding external contract.4

The engineers measured checkpoint duration, restore time, and the lag accumulated while state was being recovered. An operator with gigabytes of keyed state may need significantly longer to restart than a stateless consumer. The recovery budget must include that period.

Event Time and Late Results

The merchant report grouped orders by when the business operation occurred, called event time. That differs from processing time, the moment the analytics worker received the event. A purchase made at 10:02 but delayed until 10:36 belongs in the 10:00–10:05 window under an event-time report.

The processor needs a policy for deciding when an interval is ready to publish. A watermark is an estimate of how far event time has progressed, allowing the system to close windows under an allowed lateness policy. It is not proof that no older event will ever arrive.

Baodium permitted late corrections under a defined interval. A corrected window total carried the merchant, window, revision, and complete revised amount. A consumer of that result replaced the previous total for the same window and revision key rather than adding the new total to the old one. An event arriving after the correction limit required a separately audited repair path.

This made the reporting contract explicit. Customers could distinguish a provisional window value from a finalized one, and recovery could replay source events without adding the same purchases twice.

Testing Interruption and Recovery

Baodium’s most useful tests stopped processing between durable steps. One test crashed the task creator after its database commit and before its Kafka offset commit. The event was delivered again, and exactly one confirmation task existed afterward.

Another test stopped a sender after the provider accepted the email but before the sender saved that acceptance. The task entered UNCERTAIN, and the recovery path used the original submission identity. A provider that could not report the earlier result required the explicit duplicate-versus-missing-email policy.

The suite also exercised malformed events, missing versions, consumer rebalances, outbox relay restarts, and a projection rebuild from retained records. It verified the effects of replay, including the case in which old deduplication markers had expired.

Finally, recovery ran with new customer orders still arriving. The team measured unfinished-task age and provider acceptances until the backlog reached its expected range. Decreasing Kafka lag alone did not satisfy the test if pending work had simply accumulated in Notification Service.

Policy Events and Integration Reconciliation

The same design applies to the deployment-policy service from Chapter 11. An administrator publishes policy revision 18. Jenkins needs to enforce the active policy when it deploys, Slack needs to announce the change, and an audit worker needs the revision history.

If policy publication synchronously calls those integrations, a Slack outage can prevent administrators from publishing new rules. Instead, the policy owner commits the revision and an outbox event together. A PolicyRevisionPublished event carries the revision ID and a content digest. Each integration processes the event under its own identity and records the revision it has applied.

The policy service still owns the authoritative active revision. A Jenkins integration cannot treat a delayed event or its local copy as proof that an old approval is currently valid. At deployment time, the enforcement boundary applies the authorization and revision-validity rules from Chapter 10.

The integration dashboard compares the active revision with the revision each connector reports. A reconciliation worker periodically checks those differences and creates repair tasks before advancing its own durable checkpoint. That detects a connector that acknowledged an event but crashed before applying the change.

If Jira becomes unavailable during an approval check, the worker records INDETERMINATE and retries under the same operation identity. An event cannot grant authority by itself, and a missing approval response cannot be treated as permission to deploy.

When a Queue Is Enough

A durable queue works well when each task has a clear handler and a bounded retry policy. A database-backed state machine and scheduled workers also serve many longer operations. The operation record identifies the permitted next states, a worker claims the work, and each step commits its result before scheduling another.

A refund that waits for a human approval, contacts a provider, reconciles an uncertain response, and possibly compensates a completed action has more involved state. A workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions can coordinate timers and retries over a long period. It still needs application rules for who may authorize each step and whether an external operation can be repeated safely.

For Baodium’s notification system, the task table handled sending and provider recovery. Kafka served the independent consumers that needed a retained order-event history. The team did not need a workflow engine for every email, nor did it need Kafka merely to schedule one background task. Those choices depended on how many consumers needed the data, how long they might need to replay it, and the business effects of repeating an action.

Design Exercise: Ride-Hailing Trip Events

Consider a ride-hailing platform that publishes TripRequested, TripAccepted, TripStarted, and TripCompleted. Billing charges the rider, while a driver-earnings service prepares payouts, Notification sends receipts, and Analytics produces city-level reports.

A retained event log keyed by trip ID gives independent consumers access to trip history and keeps events for one trip in one partition under the agreed partitioning rule. A retention period covering the weekend, incident repair, and catch-up is necessary because a consumer might fail late on Friday. Seven days is a reasonable initial test case, subject to measured recovery duration and any longer audit requirement.

Billing records a durable charge intent using the trip ID and the accepted fare version as its business identity. A repeated TripCompleted event retrieves that intent rather than creating another logical charge. The provider submission uses a stable idempotency key, and a timeout enters reconciliation rather than inviting a fresh charge. Driver payouts need equivalent protection.

Now suppose a producer sends a completion event before the trip-start event. Kafka preserves that incorrect publication order faithfully. The billing consumer therefore checks the trip version and completion state, pauses an incomplete transition, or retrieves the current authoritative trip record before charging. Its correctness cannot depend only on the order in which messages appear in Kafka.

Analytics has a different recovery path. It can rebuild a city report from the retained history or an authoritative archive, applying event-time rules and corrections. Notification can create receipts from completed trip facts, but a replay must not resend every old receipt unless the repair operation explicitly requests it.

This design illustrates the choices that matter: how a business operation is identified, which order must be preserved, what the consumer commits before acknowledging input, and what effect a replay is permitted to produce.

Summary

Baodium’s Kafka consumers were current during the promotion, yet customers were waiting for confirmation emails. Notification Service had already created the tasks, while sender throughput was lower than the rate at which new tasks arrived. Looking at the oldest unfinished task and the provider’s accepted rate exposed the actual bottleneck.

The team then had to protect each boundary against interruption. The outbox made event publication recoverable, including after an uncertain broker acknowledgment. Consumer transactions prevented redelivery from creating another task. Sender identity and reconciliation addressed the harder problem of a provider that might have accepted an email whose response was lost.

Retained logs also introduced ordering, replay, and schema obligations. Those choices were useful for Catalog projections, analytics, and policy integrations, while simpler queues remained appropriate for bounded background tasks. Chapter 13 examines another way a service can return a successful response while the result itself becomes less useful: the behavior of a machine-learning system after deployment.

Assumption and scope & A committed order event can create a durable notification task, and that task can reach a recorded provider outcome without blocking checkout.
Condition that tests it & A relay loses its acknowledgment, a consumer replays an event, a sender crashes during submission, or task arrivals exceed provider throughput.
Constraint or invariant & Order confirmation and outbox intent commit together. Consumers create one task per order under database constraints. Provider acceptance and recipient delivery have separate evidence. Replay never implicitly authorizes another external effect.

000 task arrivals and 10,000 provider acceptances per minute, unfinished work grows by 2,000 per minute, or about 360,000 in three hours. Kafka lag alone did not reveal that backlog.

Signal and evaluation window & During incidents and recovery, measure outbox age, per-partition consumer lag, sender arrival and completion rates, oldest unfinished task, uncertain submissions, and dead-letter age.
Control and decision & Increase capacity only at the constrained stage. Bound accepted work and retries, reconcile uncertain submissions, and permit replay only with a defined destination and business effect.
